Wyrmspan Description: This voraciousness for milk as a hatchling is legendary. A single grazer has been known to deplete an entire lactating herd of milk, and will resort to eating whole animals after the milk runs dry.

The Genial Mothdragon has an unusually long period of altriciality. Young remain helpless for nearly half their lives, forming very strong bonds with their caretakers as a result. This attachment does not depend on the species of caretaker.
The Algal Lindworm lives in lakes and subsists off algae for most of its life. It only turns carnivorous during its brief mating season, eating fish, aquatic birds, and even the odd manatee.
Frugivorous Grazers are named for their diet, which consists entirely of fruit.
This dragon is normally friendly and docile, but slumbers deeply. If startled awake, the feydragon will attack anything in sight, including kin.
Flocks of this dragonette gather in the troposphere, and are often associated with rapid changes in weather.
Temperate Bamboo Dragons of all sexes may give birth to up to 500 hatchlings during their lives.
The wings of the Loyal Feydragon change colors depending on its mood. Never approach one with solid red wings.
The Leafeating Cricketcatcher is a popular pest control option on organic farms.
When submerged, the heat radiated by a single Melodious Firedragon egg can boil 5 liters of water (1.3 gallons) in 10 minutes.

Along with its mother's milk, Seedeating Drake hatchlings must ingest a diet of several specific plants and fruits. This special diet is believed to prepare its digestive system to handle the notoriously spicy firebird, upon which adults exclusively subsist.
As a hatchling, the Savannah Dragonette has the ability to camouflage itself to perfectly match any surrounding. This ability is lost as an adult, a phenomenon that continues to baffle dracologists.

In a remarkable example of convergent evolution, the Mellifera Feydragon looks almost identical to the humble honeybee, and was long thought to be a subspecies of Apis Mellifera. Only in 2023 did dracologists discover that it is actually a feydragon, with a complete internal skeleton (instead of an exoskeleton).
The Scavenging Cricketcatcher is endangered. In addition to being an obligate insectivore, it exclusively eats insects that are already dead before it arrives.
The Redwood Lung Dragon was named for its habitat. It burrows under the roots of redwood trees, making itself a nest that lasts for centuries.
When in flight, the Peregrine Firedragon looks like its namesake, the peregrine falcon. The main difference is that the Peregrine Firedragon also shoots fire as it flies, cooking its prey in midair.
The Common Grass Lindworm is often mistaken for a garter snake. Both species are friends to gardeners, as they keep pesky insects and rodents at bay.
As a hatchling, the Keening Amphiptere perfectly mimics an injured animal. When scavengers or potential saviors come to investigate, it pounces.

Lady Pepper's Anthology of Dragons quotes the last words of Hannah the Huntress the 2nd as follows, "Oh aren't you just the cutest? Let me put you in my purse." Lady Pepper notes, "Genetics is fascinating."
The Miniature Rex may look cute, but even as a hatchling it has sharp claws, sharper teeth, and breathes fire. Wise humans keep their distance.
Due to its uniquely other-worldly appearance, many dracologists believe that the Fae Tamarin devolved in an alternate dimension, inadvertently crossing over just a few thousand years ago.
Getting within auditory range of a Cheshire Dragon should be avoided. Travelers who encounter this dragon report feeling confused for several days afterward-that is, if they make it back at all.

The appetite of the Ravenous Granite Dragon is so great that it needs a territory of approximately eight square kilometers (2000 acres) to support each individual. As a result, these dragons meet only to briefly mate, earning them the nickname "The Lonely Hunters."

Lady Pepper's Anthology of Dragons describes the last moments of Hannah the Huntress as follows, "Hannah looked the Vampiric Horned Dragon in the eyes, and in those eyes saw a question: 'May I pretty please have a little bit of your blood?' Hannah answered the unspoken question out loud, 'Sure thing, little guy!" Lady Pepper notes, "Like father, like daughter."
An inhabitant of dank, dark woodlands, this dragon subsists almost exclusively on lichen (especially those in the genera Usnea and Cladonia).

In the Bargaining Grazer's mating ritual, two individuals present crystals, flowers, shiny rocks, and other natural baubles to each other, then engage in a lengthy trading process. If they come to an agreement, they mate for life.
The frills on this dragon wave back and forth, hypnotizing a predator as it selects a target. Once the predator is distracted, the cobrette strikes.

The Silent Cobrette is the only species of cobrette that does not produce venom. Dracologists believe that the species became so adept at hunting through stealth that its need for venom disappeared, as did its ability to produce it.

In 1991, dracologists discovered that the Singeing Remora is not an independent species after all, but actually the juvenile of the Flaming Remora. Juveniles live separately from adults, so their relationship was not properly understood until trail cameras became widely available.
Don't be fooled by this dragon's small stature! Even as an infant, the dragonette's lungs are capable of bellowing a raucous cackle that can flatten a small tree.

The Guiding Feydragon is one of the world's best trackers, and is often used by humans to assist in search and rescue activities. The feydragon can smell weeks-old trails and find buried nests months after they have been abandoned.

The Chameleon Dragonette thrives in old-growth boreal forests in polar climates. It is one of the few dragons that hibernates, and does so all winter. In the summer it subsists primarily off of mosquitoes, catching them with its 1-meter (3.3-foot) tongue.
The upward-curving tufts around this dragon's jaws give it the appearance of a permanent smile. This should not, however, be confused with actual friendliness.

Many pet stores sell Kindly Sea Serpents to unsuspecting parents in place of a gerbil or hamster. Taking on a Kindly Sea Serpent as a pet is strongly discouraged. This long-lived species always outlives the interest of the child, and often outlives the child as well.

Lawndrakes are common in suburban habitats and have an amazing capacity to find lost jewelry and other valuables. The Lawndrake will ultimately give these items back to their owners, but not until the owner has sufficiently earned the privilege.
This species can most often be spotted "patrolling" seaside cliffs. Its tumbling flight pattern-which comes from riding ocean breezes- is the species' most distinctive characteristic.
The Subterranean Basilisk's effective camouflage, preference for remote caves, and elusive nature means that it was not classified until 1988.

The Swift Lung Dragon is widely considered to be one of the most helpful species of dragon. Several popular dragon fables (including Finding Oasis in Desert and Escape from Lion) are based on interactions with this species.
The Weary Gryphdragon's large body mass and small wings make it it a poor flyer. Although this species nests in large trees for protection at night, it spends most of its waking hours on the ground.
Fossils that look virtually identical in morphology to the Aged Sea Serpent have been found dating back over 200 million years.
The tiny Striped Dragonette weighs a mere 0.3 kg (11 ounces).
The Great Golden Lung Dragon typically rises at dawn. Catching a glimpse of one in the morning light is considered a sign of good fortune.

On several occasions, hikers have reported being guided to safety by a "blue ghost." In each report, the ghost silently appears, identifies a path to safety, then disappears. Dracologists hypothesize that these "ghosts" were Blue Forest Spirits.
The Tawny Northern Drake's mottled coat changes with the seasons, from white in the winter to a golden brown in the summer.
Despite its fearsome appearance, the Tranquil Wyrm presents little threat to humans. Unless cornered, individuals will flee instead of engaging in conflict.

Laying only 1 egg every two years, the rare Rainbow Guardian is fiercely protective of its eggs. On several instances, unwary hikers have been forced to flee after accidentally wandering too close to a Guardian's nest.

Especially well-adapted for hunting at night, the Owlatic Amphiptere is a terror to small nocturnal animals. One adult is capable of eating over 1000 dragonmice each year, in addition to the occasional olivaceous possum snack.

Surprisingly light and fast for its size, the Spry Horned Lung Dragon is well known for teasing humans by flying in close, then whisking away at the last moment. Its playful and mischievous nature delights most humans, though it would be a mistake to consider this dragon "tame" or "gentle."
Average in every way, this lung dragon often fills the early chapters of Dracology 101 textbooks.
Despite its small stature, the Wise Anteldragon can often be seen presiding over a thunder of dragons of all types. What discussions (if any) take place during these sessions is unknown to humans.
The Aloof Gryphdragon can be summoned with an onyx amulet, but finds the practice to be extremely offensive.
In contrast to its nearest relative (the Spry Horned Lung Dragon), the smaller Chromatic Blue Lung Dragon prefers to stay out of sight and remain undisturbed.
The Tawny Steppe Wyvern enjoys human music. Outdoor concerts of all types attract an audience of this species, listening from the rafters or soaring above the venue.

In the early 1200s, Sir Conner tended to an injured member of this species in his garden. To this day, its descendants keep a watchful eye over the garden (now a public park) and make sure that no humans there come to harm.
Named after the Greater Calm Loch, this serpent primarily lives in deep underwater crevasses only coming out to feed at night.
The Hoarding Flyer is often disparagingly called the seagull of dragons. Members have been known to steal sandwiches and other food from unsuspecting picnickers.
Although this species is not especially long-lived, special genetic memory grants hatchlings the inherited knowledge and skills of their ancestors.
Although this species tends to keep to itself, it has a notoriously short fuse when provoked, often with deadly consequences.

The Haughty Wyvern is easily spooked. Its "haughty" moniker comes not any arrogance, but because this dragon is often seen with its chin in the air, as it escapes from nearby predators (or dracologists).
Often mistaken for a jaguar, the Stealthy Rufftail can be identified by its slightly darker coloration and bright red tail.
Dracologists believe they are able to trace the history the Primeval Wyrm back to the Permian period, almost 300 million years ago.
The Descending Firevern has among the hottest flames and longest reaches of dragons.

The Guarding Horned Drake is very possessive and does not tolerate theft of anything within its purview. For this reason, individuals of this species (primarily males) are excellent caretakers of hatchlings left in their care.
Thanks to its stone-like coloring and the intricate pattern of its scales, the Scaly Rock Dragon is a master of camouflage and is well-suited to mountainous regions.
Endowed with extraordinarily keen senses, this dragon has been known to forecast storms and provide warnings of imminent seismic activity.
While this dragon cannot fly, males use their wings to intimidate aggressors and attract mates. In females, wings are believed to be vestigial.
Since the beginning of reliable recordkeeping, circa 1850, there have been no known instances of an Ancient One dying of natural causes or even showing signs of degenerative aging.
Large and aggressive, these dragons are frequently disruptive to human settlements. They have been known to torch structures to create a diversion, then consume livestock in the ensuing chaos.
Extremely elusive, these dragons live up to their name with an almost supernatural ability to anticipate intruders, typically fleeing long before the intruder arrives.
A highly adept hunter, the Patient Redwyrm has been known to lie in wait for its prey for hours or even days.

Several ancient cultures have viewed the Multicolor Flyer with reverence. According to legend, it was gifted all the colors of the rainbow by the Dragon God as a reward for services rendered in ancient times.

Dracologists disagree on the Primordiasaur's evolutionary relationship to other modern dragons. The prevailing theory links it to the sea serpents, but vocal dissidents argue that it is more closely related to the wyrms.

The webbed wings of this dragon make it both an excellent flyer and swimmer. This dragon can seamlessly transition from the air to the water, although it prefers to stay hidden in the shallow waters of marshes and fens.
This species is on the edge of extinction even with extensive human intervention. This drake has intensely anti-social tendencies, which even extend to the majority of potential mates.
This rockbreaker lives up to its name by using its powerful jaws to crush and clear out solid rock for nests typically built into high limestone cliffs.
The Keen Cricketcatcher's sharp claws are used solely for climbing trees in search of dragonworms, as well as grubs and other insects.
This dragon is a particular menace to farmers. Its voracious appetite and extreme tenacity mean that one individual can gradually consume an entire heard of cattle over a period of weeks or months.
Although most wyverns are haughty, this species is particularly so.

This gryphdragon gets its name from its ancestors' protection of the Commons during medieval times. In exchange for protecting animals grazing in the Commons, humans gave the gryphdragon food during harvest, establishing an enduring symbiotic relationship.
The Hawkish Firevern's name is something of a misnomer. The dragon shares a common ancestor with the modern-day falcon, which helps explain its ability to fly at near-supersonic speeds.

This species can remain virtually motionless for hours, and is well adapted living alongside humans in urban environments. On more than one occasion, a Stoic Gryphdragon has been mistaken for a gargoyle, much to the surprise of passersby.

The most striking feature of this dragon is its wings, which ironically look like leaves from maple trees. It is thought that mistake originated from a translation error, which was not identified until the moniker "Oak-Wing" was already widespread.

Named for their singularly playful temperament, the Spirited Firevern is a highly energetic species. As many as 12 individuals have been seen flying in incredibly intricate, perfectly synchronized displays. The purpose of these displays remains unknown.
This species is poorly understood, as few have ever gotten close enough to study it.
Named after the colorful koi fish it imitates, this species is known for hoarding large caches of shiny objects from gold nuggets to tin foil.
The Northern Cavalier Wyvern is a master at gliding. Individuals spend virtually their whole lives in the air, only landing for a few months each decade to lay and hatch eggs.
The Equatorial Cavalier Wyvern has a migratory pattern that circumnavigates the globe around the Equator.
The Speedy Lung Dragon changes directions extremely quickly. It is thought that this adaptation co-evolved with its primary food source: the marlin.

In regions where it is native, the long-lived Erudite Lung Dragon is regarded as a herald of wisdom and scholarship. As such, it is often seen on a variety of objects from ancient family crests to modern company logos.
The Protective Amphiptere is a creature of routine. Each day is made up of six strictly scheduled segments, three of which are "playtime."

Although this dragon cannot understand speech (to the best of dracologists' knowledge), it does have an uncanny ability to sense human tone and intent. A surefire way to upset this dragon is to call it "ordinary" to its face!
Rather than breathing fire, the Territorial Spitter has developed highly acidic saliva that is used as a projectile to deter rivals or protect its territory.
From a distance, this coatl is often mistaken for a bird. Only up close can it be observed that the dragon is scaled instead of feathered, from the tip of its nose to its distinctive tail scales.
The Northern Gryphdragon is often seen at higher elevations, which may explain why it was chosen for the sigil of the Guild of Highlands.
Ironically, the favorite snack of this dragon is the olive branch, the traditional sign of peace.

Males of this species attract females through elaborate courtship rituals, in which they fly in elaborate patterns, letting sunlight glisten off their bright blue scales. To keep their scales shiny, males spent significant time grooming, rightly earning the name "fastidious."

The Dappled Glade Spirit is a keystone species in many old-growth forests. Its high body-temperature is critical for wearing down the protective coating on many of the seeds and nuts that it consumes.

Adaptability is one of the primary hallmarks of Little Amphiptere. Although the species tends to avoid locations with high human density, it tolerates a wide range of climates, from temperate to tropical.
The Nimble Trilling Amphiptere is rarely seen but often heard. Its primary call, a high-pitched "kekekeke" that is used to herd prey, can be heard up to 2.5 kilometers (1.5 miles) away.

Unfortunately, the first dracologist to study this wyrm, Hans the Hunter the 2nd, learned that it was highly venomous (RIP). It wasn't until several decades later that a second dracologist, Hans the Hunter the 3rd, discovered that it was also highly poisonous (RIP).
The Magnificent Amphiptere is best known for its impressive plumage, found on both males and females. This plumage is made of feathers instead of scales, which is uncommon in the dragon world.
The Pocket Amphiptere is one of the smallest species of amphiptere. Adults weigh just over 3 grams (0.11 ounces).
The Miserly Amphiptere lives in relatively barren regions where food is scarce. This scarcity likely explains this species' aggressive tendencies in protecting its (meager) food supplies.

This species migrates several thousand kilometers every year, from subarctic climates in summer, to temperate forests and grasslands in the winter. Its diet is similarly varied; it eats mostly hares and flaming foxes in summer, and rabbits and dracosquirrels in the winter.

This shy mountain species is the most recent dragon to be identified, with final classification completed in late 2023. This species does not yet have a Guild-approved common name, nor is it likely to have one any time soon. In an attempt at humor, the Forest Guild named this dragon after Australopithecus, a genus of human ancestors. The Plains Guild and the Guild of Highlands took offense, and refuse to approve a common name until the Forest Guild fixes this "affront to humanity." An official spokesperson for the Forest Guild called the other two guilds "humorless dingbats," though in retrospect, this statement was perhaps intended to be off the record.
The Minor Sharpclaw has major attitude. Although it is too small to do much damage, it makes itself such a nuisance that other species steer clear.

This drake has been known to "help" hikers, by carefully guiding them into gullies and trenches, then turning them around and refusing to show them the exit. It is believed that the drake finds human struggles to be entertaining.

Throughout much of human history Good Drakes formed symbiotic relationships with humans in hunter-gatherer camps, warning humans of incoming predators in exchange for leftover food. Although they are not "domesticated" to the extent that dogs are, there are some (largely within the Plains Guild) who still keep Good Drakes as pets.

Amateur dragonwatchers often risk life and limb to view the flight displays of the Bellicose Firevern. Dragonwatching guides strongly recommend that interested parties seek out the Spirited Firevern instead, as this species offers a similarly impressive display at significantly lower risk.
The Stalking Drake travels in packs and, much like a hyena, eats a combination of carrion and live prey (including rats and dragonmice).
Whenever the Penurious Red Wyrm catches more prey than it needs, it caches the food for storage deep in climate-controlled caves. The food may remain there for months or even years.
The Variegated Amphiptere is typically found in the company of the Mosaic Guardian. It is believed that the amphiptere helps rear the larger dragon's hatchlings in exchange for protection.
This rockbreaker is often heard but rarely seen. It makes a distinctive crunching sound as it chews rock to build an ever-growing network of caverns in search of rare purple crystals.
This amphiptere often follows in the wake of the Shaly Rockbreaker, scarfing up any leftover crystal shards that the larger dragon leaves behind.

The Custodial Koiwyrm builds elaborate nests, with nary a feather or twig out of place. In fact, a koiwyrm will gift leftover food to nearby creatures, rather than sully the pristineness of its living space.
The Splitting Golden Hydra is the only known species with a bifurcated cerebrum, which evenly splits the hydra's cognitive processes across two nearly identical heads.
It wasn't until the early 2010s that all guilds finally agreed that the Antediluvian Basilisk was, in fact, a dragon. The Guild of Highlands was the last holdout, claiming that it was a snake.

When necessary, the Spirited Hydrapere can reproduce through budding. The head is the first piece to grow, followed by the tail, then the thorax. In contrast to the Splitting Golden Hydra, the two heads belong to two individuals-who don't necessarily see eye to eye.
The Chameleon Coatl can control the angle of its scales to within a fraction of a degree, allowing it to reproduce any color.

Generations of selective breeding have decreased the Knowing Guardian's size and created a docile and trainable species. It is a favorite for personal companionship-but only for those with plenty of space!

Everything about this species is baffling to dracologists, including its combination of fur, scales, and feathers; its frigid body temperature of 42 degrees Celsius (107 degrees Fahrenheit); and its apparent ability to absorb nutrients from the air.

This species is blustering but ultimately harmless. It can most reliably be distinguished from its venomous lookalike cousin, the Selfish Lung Dragon, by the green markings on the underside of its claws-but we don't recommend getting close enough to check.

Known to attack other creatures for food, shelter, or water (or for no discernible reason at all), the Selfish Lung Dragon lives a solitary life, occasionally partnering with a mate for a short time but otherwise living alone.
Often found in the company of the Variegated Amphiptere, this species that never stops moving. Legend has it that they tirelessly patrol the world, ready to defend it against threats new or old.
Colloquially known as "Red Zorro" the Red Guardian commonly gifts food to species it believes to be inferior, including humans.
Despite its large size, the Quartzy Rockbreaker is surprisingly nimble. It can squeeze through impossibly small holes, presumably due to its ability to dislocate most of its joints.
Despite its large size, the Capricious Venomous Wyrm mostly eats small creatures, including mice (both dragonmice and standard mice), voles, small birds, and the young of its enemies.

The harvesting of dragon venom was outlawed by the Dragon Protection Act of 1972. However, the Sharp-Tongued Spitter faces significant poaching from humans as its venom remains a prized ingredient in several traditional cuisines. (The flavor of the venom can only be described by enthusiasts as tasting of "yellow.")
The Red-Crested Gryphdragon often forms packs with misfit members of other dragon species.
The Smirking Ridgeback's pronounced underbite lends its jaw the strength needed to crush granite, its favorite food.
The Titanic Coatl has one of the highest internal body temperatures of all known dragons at 93° Celsius (200° Fahrenheit). As such, one of the primary threats to this species is cold temperatures.
Small but sneaky, the Lilliputian Fae works in groups to distract and overpower both invaders and prey.
This wyvern was named posthumously for the nineteenth-century dracologist Nangula Sossusvlei, who still holds the record for cataloging the most dragon species in history.
The Customary Grazer has an exceptionally slow metabolism, eating only once every 3-4 weeks. That said, its six stomachs have a huge capacity, so when it does eat, it eats a lot.

The initial name proposed for this dragon was the Napoleonic Firevern, due to a combination of its small stature and aggressive personality. The Guild of Highlands found the name in poor taste and vetoed it. Ultimately, the guilds agreed to "churlish."
The Impenetrable Redwyrm has a tough exterior, but its loyalty is widespread in the myths and legends of several cultures.
The Starlit Shepherd is one of the friendliest species of dragons. To these wonderful and innocent creatures, each stranger is a new best friend unless proven otherwise.

The Kind Mistvern has been known to raise the orphaned young of other species of dragons. The foster dragons it raises largely take on the personality of the Kind Mistvern, typically making them kinder and gentler than others of their species.

When the Oracular Dragon is asleep, it breathes with a heavy wheeze that sounds much like a human whispering. Travelers who have managed to approach one without waking it report hearing mysterious prophecies, most of which ultimately come to pass.
Most species of rockbreaker use their powerful jaws to dig the tunnels that they call home. The Rocky Rockbreaker, on the other hand, does the majority of its digging with its curiously strong toes.

The Sea Viper can best be described in the words of Captain Tucker, who narrated an encounter with one as follows, "Well, something was struggling, and lord help me when it came out of the water I was sure we were goners. It tore right through the net and burned a hole clean through my boat. I got insurance after that."

Statues of the Royal Wyvern have greeted guests at noble weddings throughout history. It is unknown how this trend began. Although the statues are a symbol of serenity, the temperament of the wyvern itself is very much the opposite.
Although normally dull gray in appearance, the back scales of the Lavender Feydragon take on a brilliant lavender color during its two-week mating season.
The Playful Hornwyrm's fondness for cow's milk and sugarcane can make ice cream hard to find in certain equatorial regions, particularly during its nursing season.
Each spot on a Southern Mammoth RidgeDragon's wing is believed to represent one hatchling that it has successfully launched into the world.

The Crafty Moray was a common figurehead carved into the bows of sailing vessels during the 17th and 18th centuries. Having such a figurehead was believed to ensure good weather and provide safe passage.

This species became widely domesticated after it was discovered that a strong electric current runs through the fae, providing enough energy to replace a medium-sized generator. The Dragon Protection Act of 1972 sets strict standards for humane working conditions for the Steely Fae.

Unlike other wyverns, the horns of the Great Horned Wyvern change color depending on when it last ate. A dark color indicates that the wyvern has just eaten, whereas a pale color means that it may be on the prowl.
The Ophidian Recluse has only been sighted twice in recorded history (both times by members of the Rainforest Guild). Dracologists are divided on whether it exists at all.

The Aerial Recluse spends most of its time at an altitude of 9,000 to 12,000 meters (approximately 30,000 to 40,000 feet). Although it typically stays well away from humans, its mating season frequently disrupts air travel.
With its incredibly strong jaws and sharp teeth, an infant of this species was once observed biting a diesel locomotive in half. The infant was thought to be teething.
When startled, males make the characteristic "shriek" that gave the species its name. Thus, it is not surprising that females do the majority of a pack's hunting.
The Blue Keeper's favorite color is orange. This species has been known to follow around hunters wearing orange vests, much to the chagrin of the hunters and to the delight of their prey.
The Contrary Lung Dragon received its name for its call, which sounds eerily like, "Nononono NOOOOOOOOO!"
Viewed from the front, this dragon seems almost otherworldly, with its bright coloring and ethereal plumage. Viewed from the back, it is very dull and very plainly a Wyvern.
Although not related to the Tawny Frogmouth, this dragon is known for consuming small rodents, insects, and just about anything else they can get their mouths around.

Lady Pepper's Anthology of Dragons quotes the last words of Tybalt the Tracker as follows, "Ach! Hans, run! It's the Wily Lindworm!" Lady Pepper notes, "A good man died that day, and for what purpose?"

The tiny Brushwood Dragonette makes its home in the forest undergrowth, evading predators by hiding in thick brambles. Rarely flying, it uses its tall wings to carry bundles of twigs on its back, taking its nest wherever it goes.
The Jaunty Dragonette was named for its unique sashaying walk. If dragons could be runway models, this species would be the star of the show.

Prior to the Dragon Protection Act of 1972, the Brushtail Fey was hunted for its long tail, which was used to adorn hats. To this day, these hats occasionally appear on the secondary market, though at an astronomical cost.
Lady Pepper's Anthology of Dragons quotes the last words Hans the Hunter as follows, "Hey, you don't look so tough!" Lady Pepper notes, "Hans the Hunter was a moron."
Its "Cosmic" name comes not from any otherworldly reason, but from the glimmering of the gems and scales on its back.
The Reticent Manta glows vividly under ultraviolet light thanks to pigments in its scales. This discovery was made entirely by accident.
The Metamorphic Feydragon can take on the appearance of any dragon, but cannot change its size. Any small dragon could potentially be a Metamorphic Feydragon in disguise.
It is widely believed that the Clairvoyant Feydragon can read minds.
Though this dragon does have a bone-chilling laugh, its name actually comes from its diet of 100% hyena meat.

After the President of the Dragon Guilds called the Homely Fae "one ugly beast," teenagers around the world turned the Homely Fae into their mascot, as a sign of (very low-key and poorly coordinated) rebellion.
Affectionately referred to as a "Trash Panda" by urbanites, this species enjoys digging through garbage even more than its (ringtail) raccoon namesake.

The Diving Moray has been known to wreak havoc on military submarines for entertainment. It uses electromagnetic pulses to distort sonar, and often taps out a distracting "ka-thunk-a-thunk" on the hull, sometimes for hours on end.
A master of disguise, the Vanishing Creeper can alter the pattern on its wings to blend in with nearly any background.
The Macabre Lindworm is known for decorating its vestigial wings with the entrails of prey to attract potential mates.
Now considered an invasive species throughout much of the world, the Augural Fae was intentionally distributed by humans in a misguided attempt to control dragonmice populations.
Also known as Diver's Bane, the Solitary Remora kicks up dust clouds from the sea floor whenever a human is spotted. By the time the dust clears, the remora is gone.
The spread of the invasive kudzu has greatly reduced numbers of the Steadfast Southern Drake. Kudzu is highly toxic to the species, but tastes delicious to them.

Due to their attraction to light and high-altitude flight patterns, these mothdragons are often spotted by airline passengers circling their planes at night. Pilots learn to ignore them, even though their aerial acrobatics initially appear threatening to flight safety.

The Gnawing Seraph is named for its parasitic feeding method: It latches onto larger prey, drinking its fill before moving on. The seraph's saliva is numbing to most animals, so it is able to feast and disappear long before its host notices that anything is amiss.
It is widely believed that the Dowsing Fae has an innate ability to locate water. It does not.
Watchful Wyverns nest around dormant volcanoes, where they appear to be watching and waiting. Their presence is thought to keep volcanoes dormant. They are nearly extinct.
This dragon likes children and dogs, and is thought to have a preternatural ability to calm both. That said, one cry (or one bark) and the Nurturing Feydragon disappears.
This dragon lures crickets by mimicking their chirps, turning them one by one into cricketcatcher snacks.
This dragon is known for its bright colors and flashy, flightless wings. However, despite its beauty it is notoriously clumsy, and has even been known to knock over its own nest.
Waddy's Rufftail was discovered by Messieurs Waddington and Biddy of the Plains Guild. In a move that some regard as gauche, the duo named the species with a portmanteau of their own names.
The Warming Firevern often comes to the aid of frozen travelers. Unfortunately, accepting this aid is risky: There's a fine line between toasty and just toast.
These small dragons are known for stalking small insects, sometimes spending hours following a moth, only to lose interest immediately upon catching it.
These dragons possess a gentle and approachable nature. Their distinctive glass-like scales readily reflect light, casting a shimmering spectrum of colors as they soar through the sky.
Well known for its combative nature, this amphiptere instigates fights by antagonizing and taunting fellow dragons and intimidates other creatures by displaying its retractable spikes and vast wings.

Distinct from other acid-spitting dragons, the Sagacious Spitter uses its acidic saliva for melting stone in caves to prepare a recessed nest for its mate and clutch of eggs. Its surprisingly amenable nature has even allowed dracologists to peacefully harvest its spit for use in alchemical concoctions.

Like its cousin, the Reticent Manta, the Speckled Manta glows in ultraviolet light. This manta generates it own ultraviolet source from its horns to make a brilliant golden glow that is blinding to adversaries and adventurers alike. Use of protective lenses is recommended when encountering a Speckled Manta.

Often mistaken for Custodial Koiwyrms at first sight because of their beautiful and complex nests, these majestic wyrms can sometimes be seen atop towers working at... something with their forelimbs. Some townsfolk swear they're destructive, while one historian claims that a falsekoi fixed a hole in a bell tower's roof with one of its own scales.

Fond of playing tricks on humans, this jokester makes snorting sounds that are oddly reminiscent of laughter. Dracologists are advised to watch this wyvern closely, given its uncanny ability to fling objects with its prehensile tail.
This dragon is known for crafting near-invisible lairs dug out of small rocky outcroppings. The entrance to these lairs is often less than half the width of the owner's head.

The Northern Pane Dragon derives its name from its prismatic scales, which refract sunlight as it flies, resembling stained-glass window segments. Some ambitious historians credit this dragon as the inspiration for the stained-glass art form.
Dracologists believe that this dragon's breath is so hot that it melts gold ingots to roll in, adding sheen to its otherwise gray, bland scales.

Originally believed to be an adolescent of the Green Ghost, the Verdant Wisp still retains a spectral name in reference to its larger relative. Unlike its namesake, however, the wisp uses its foliate wings primarily for camouflage.

The Bullish Gryphdragon's powerful wings make it adept at snatching eggs, which are a main component of its diet, from other dragons' lairs. In rare cases, it will decide not to eat the egg and raise the hatchling as its own.

When startled, this dragon emits an aroma that is vaguely reminiscent of maple syrup. Dracologists have yet to ascertain the utility of this action, but it remains delightful nevertheless. Although deliberate attempts to elicit this startle response led to sanction as part of the Dragon Protection Act of 1972, the Northwestern Auric Dragon nevertheless appears to relish the attention.

Acrobatic Horndragons are celebrated for their choreographed flight formations. Following a leader, flocks of horndragons fly wing-to-wing as they perform barrel rolls, mirror each other, soar to dizzying heights, and plummet back to the ground.

The Galvanic Wyrm can build up an electric charge from its copper-infused horns. It uses this charge to both repel enemies with electric shocks and also to create a magnetic field that attracts dragons (of all species) to its cavern. What it does with those dragons is unknown.

This cousin of the Penurious Red Wyrm can sometimes be seen leading livestock and young dragons off cliffs and to their doom by flicking its long tail in hypnotic patterns. These activities appear to be for sport, as the dragon has an herbivorous diet.

Dracologists noticed that the Directing Violet Lung Dragon likes to guide adventurers to their next task, much like a theatrical director instructs actors. A wise adventurer always says "thank you" when walking by and declines to ever give the dragon notes.

Unlike its relative, the Savanna Dragonette, this petite dragon is incapable of camouflaging itself at any age. It generally survives by appearing affable and cooperative, but be warned: When this dragon feels cornered, its mild facade drops and the claws come out.

The Fawlcora is one of the few dragons that exhale blue flame and, perhaps due to this rarity, is believed to be lucky. Explorers who have met these dragons find life always just seems to work in their favor for the next few days.
The Enlightened Feydragon is always on a quest for knowledge; some rare specimens have even taken up residence at libraries or other educational institutions to further their own erudite escapades.

The Radiant Boreal Dragonette plays a vital part in the maintenance and regeneration of healthy forest ecosystems. Although apparently unwittingly, this species causes small, low-intensity fires through a fascinating exothermic reaction in its footpads. These small burns ultimately prevent larger and more destructive forest fires.

This dragonette was nearly hunted to extinction in the 1300s for its wings, which when processed into a paste are said to have antiaging properties (a claim which has never been validated). The dragonette has since been recognized as endangered and is protected under the Dragon Protection Act of 1972.

Named for its frog-like mouth and large eyes, this dragon is a quick learner, able to repeat a behavior flawlessly after observing it only once. By adulthood, its fledgling tail shrinks and is reabsorbed into the body, while its wings become broad and muscular.
It is believed that the Naryoon Marsh Dragon is a crossbreed of the Marshy Webbed Dragon and the Contrary Lung Dragon. Its call, interestingly, sounds like "NAR-yooooooon!"
Bounding through prairies, this exuberant dragon pounces on fellow feydragons for sheer amusement. Lacking physical strength, it compensates by hypnotizing both predator and prey.

With their sharp sense of smell, these gryphdragons are exceptional at locating food and instinctively gather provisions for themselves and any creature they consider family or friend. While they primarily drink milk (of any kind) they occasionally surprise others with unique treats like crunchy dried lichen or tart berries to share.

The unique geometry of the Iridescent Lindworm's scales lend it an endlessly shifting coloration of striking blues, greens, and gem tones that some have described as a "prismatic waterfall." Ironically, this brilliant visual display means that this naturally reserved creature is highly sought among both dracologists and amateur dragon watchers.

Named both for the color of its wings and its affinity for flowers, this small fae tends to hide among blooming plants. The petal-like lashes around its eyes routinely make it a startling, if harmless, surprise to hapless flower pickers.

The Kaleidoscopic Dragonette's dense, variegated scales morph into a new pattern with every muscle movement. Though it shares 99% of its DNA with the Flocking Dragonette, this dragon flies much closer to the planet's surface and is considered to be something of a daredevil.

Long thought to be extinct, the Hovering Polychromatic Stripling was only recently rediscovered. Although their known breeding population remains relatively low, it is now believed to have reached healthy levels thanks to concerted efforts by the Y.R. Tillotson Draconic Conservation Society.

Similar to its cousin, the Leafeating Cricketcatcher, this dragon is a popular pest control option, although it is fiercer and more unpredictable. Individuals enjoy chasing and chomping several species of dracobeetle.

Retracting its gossamer wings, this palm-sized amphibious dragon plunges into the ocean, propelling itself underwater with webbed front feet. While its name reflects the innocent look found in its eyes, the Guileless Dragonette is actually a cunning hunter, able to take down aquatic life ten times its size.
The Jejune Firedragon is commonly found trying to goad other dragons into chasing it through the skies. It has far more energy than most and will often wear out both playmates and predators.

These tiny, reclusive dragons have developed the ability to communicate telepathically with others of their kind. They use their gift to gather in small groups where they sit in quietude, savoring each other's peaceful presence.

Although primarily a carnivore, this aggressive creature demonstrates a marked taste for apples (of all things). Large numbers of Precocious Amphipteres can be found in orchards during the autumnal months, sound asleep, having gorged themselves on slightly fermented fallen apples. Dracologists agree that this is generally the safest time to approach and observe this dragon, although it does not afford them much insight into their more active behaviors.
The Blooming Sharpclaw is easily enticed thanks to its curiosity, but those living near its home often find themselves irritated by its constant, high-pitched cries.
While other ridgedragon breeds are often identified by their spotted wings, the Prime Flighty Ridgedragon is best known for the deep purple coloration of its ridge horns.

This small variety of gryphdragon takes delight in surrounding itself with an assortment of other, larger dragons. Originally thought to be for protection, this behavior is now believed to be purely social.
Vibrantly colored and full of energy, this boisterous mini-dragon is always ready for a game. When alone, it invents its own fun activities and eagerly tries to entice any nearby creature to join in.

The Leopard Cobrette's coloring, similar to many poisonous amphibians, warns predators to stay away. Its wide wings have a waterproof coating that allows it to dive into lakes and catch fish almost as large as itself.

The global population of Omnigobblers is low, which is probably a good thing, given that each eats at least 13 times its weight daily. Gastroliths in their seven-chambered stomachs make short work of even the toughest materials, and they have been known to happily eat rocks, hardwoods, and even large pieces of metal with no apparent ill effect.
The Famished Fae Dragonette has an insatiable appetite. Despite its small size, the dragonette never seems to get full; it's almost as if its stomach is in another dimension.

Spending much of their waking hours creating and perfecting their "song," these dragons collaborate to harmonize their voices. By manipulating sound waves, they can shift stone and earth to construct their homes.

These dragons have a curious nature that leads them to seek out food that might put up a fight. While they primarily eat plants, they take particular delight in snacking on insectivorous varieties, such as a Venus flytrap and cobra lily.

Clangorous Feydragons gather in trees during their mating season. The males create a cacophonous uproar with their wings and tails in a ritual to attract females, sounding similar to a swarm of locusts.

Adults of this small breed are horrible parents. They typically leave their eggs in Spotted Licheneater nests instead of caring for them. Due to this strange behavior, their young have evolved to look nearly identical to their foster parents until adolescence, at which point their wings and eyerings distinguish them from their adopted siblings.

Broods of Imperious Wyverns have a distinct pecking order, with one alpha in each family group. The behavior is similar to that of chickens or other fowl, although an Imperious Wyvern would, no doubt, be outraged by the comparison.

The well-known epic poem "Red Finn and the Sunlight's Lament" is an homage to this dragon's striking plumage. The author's follow-up offering, a novelty limerick entitled "That's not a Drake, A-Moray," garnered significantly less critical acclaim and effectively ended their literary career.

These whimsical and slightly mischievous dragons are notorious for wandering off in the woods, captivated by any creature or sparkly item that piques their interest. Much like the Bargaining Grazer, they like to hunt and barter for treasures in their spare time.
The Guilded Whiskered Serpent has a very strong motherly instinct and will gracefully fill in as a foster parent for any needy fledgling.

This dragon's harsh, rigid exterior combined with its tendency to follow human travelers for miles at a time has made it feared in rural communities. It wasn't until 1910 that a dracologist was bold enough to allow a Relentless Spine Drake to catch up to him in the wild and study the result. The dracologist survived the encounter with a charming tale and a new best friend.

An attractive dragon known for its deep indigo fur and crimson feathers, the Diminutive Pegasus Dragon is unwisely kept as a pet worldwide. When children ride this horse-like creature through the house, it whips its tail around, knocking over furniture and shattering breakable items.

When it doesn't get its way, the Obstinate Plumed Coatl defiantly harumphs, paralyzes its body, and refuses to make eye contact, becoming as stiff and mute as a statue. When it has entered this state, dracologists are advised to leave it be, as the alternative can be quite unpleasant.

The Merciful Sea Serpent is a misnomer. While they prefer a damp cave environment, they are not, in fact, a sea serpent of any kind. The first explorer to identify this dragon was likely suffering from dehydration and mistook its beautiful blue scales for a secret underground lake. It wasn't until much later that the mistake was realized.

Dense alabaster feathers provide both camouflage and warmth for this glacier-dwelling dragon, which is renowned for its intricate, swooping flight pattern. In recent years, rising temperatures and glacier recession have accelerated habitat loss, landing the Andean Coatl on the endangered species list.

The Southern Cavalier Wyvern stays aloft from sunrise to sunset by gliding on thermal updrafts. To date, no one has ascertained where they disappear to once night has fallen, though it is widely believed that they shelter in an as-yet-undiscovered communal grotto.

Gifted with seemingly endless patience, the Phlegmatic Firedragon is famous for its meticulous and lengthy process of rearing its young. The species has even been known to foster orphaned hatchlings, training them in flight, hunting, and migration patterns as though they were its own offspring. As such, this dragon became the famous mascot of one of the most popular parenting magazines in publication.

The Ancient Kasei Wyvern likes to prepare fledglings in the art of combat through a sink or swim approach (literally). It deems any injuries gained in training to be part of the learning process. If it doesn't kill you, then it makes you stronger... right?
Hailing from the same regions as the Miniature Rex, the Pliant Floral Rex is adept at hiding in fields of wildflowers to ambush its favored prey, the hummingbird.
The Eastern Lupine Serpent always makes its home near that of another, larger dragon, scavenging from the kills of their more sizable brethren.

With an exceptional memory for perceived grievances, this irritable lindworm hisses and spits venom at anything, living or otherwise, that has "wronged" it. Its eyesight is well adapted to the extreme darkness of deep caves, where it prefers living a solitary existence over dealing with the frustrating behaviors of other dragons.

Though this dragon is well known as an excellent hunter, it will spare its prey surprisingly often, needing only to eat once every few weeks. Dracologists believe it may derive self-satisfaction from its hunting prowess.

The Decimating Drakeeater is one of the most vicious and dangerous dragons, hunting other dragon species exclusively to fulfill its voracious appetite. This species has been well documented as the cause of extinction for several smaller draconic species.
The Lively Tusked Lung Dragon is much more sociable than some other lung dragon species, often living in large groups that disrupt local econystems and devastate local livestock populations.

The Vivacious Amphiptere is blessed with boundless energy, allowing it to take to the skies day and night without ceasing. Its curling wings have been said to predict the weather, with the shimmering hue of its feathers becoming dim and caliginous before a storm, hence the adage, "hope for bright wings," that is commonly said before weddings, festivals, and other outdoor events.
One of the most territorial of the firevern species, the Quarrelsome Firevern creates concentric rings of burned vegetation around its chosen home to warn away any others who may encroach.
The Archaic Striated Serpent has one of the longest known lifespans of dragons. This serpent gains a stripe for every decade of existence. One was found to have over 350 striations.

Taking the safety of every young dragon in its charge very seriously, this psuedodrake builds cave-like structures out of stone and mud with its tail. These makeshift caves provide a safe haven for young dragon families during migration, allowing them to travel across vast distances securely.

Solicitous Coatls often establish themselves as matriarchs or patriarchs in seemingly disparate groups of dragons. Their ability to align natural dragon behaviors to a unified mission has also made them remarkably renowned for their proficiency in leading teambuilding exercises.

According to legend, this dragon has tiny reflective spots on its wings that depict actual celestial bodies in the universe. These spots, typically only visible at night, shine brightly in the moonlight.

Flair-this dragon's got it! This wyvern likes to show off with lots and lots of pizazz; when it's not dancing and prancing, you can often find it training others in unique routines. This is a dragon that knows what it's worth (quite a lot!).

This dragon has only been described once in the literature, by Queen Poppy the Naive herself. Although her account dates from the 1300s, Queen Poppy's descriptions were so complete that dracologists even today consider them to be accurate.

The Cyclopean Basilisk grows to such a tremendous size that smaller creatures such as Fanged Feydragons can often be spotted sleeping in various nooks across its surface. The Cyclopean may not, in fact, even be a true basilisk, but its sheer size and aggressive temperament has made a rigorous study impractical. Given this, its current taxonomic status is more a matter of convenience than of fact.

Although not mean by nature, this giant's protective instincts can be dangerous when young dragons are under its charge. Greatwyrms often become combative in the role of overseeing the horde, especially when protecting eggs or newly hatched young.

Also called the Gentle Giants of the Forest, these easygoing wyverns are in the same genus as Dappled Glade Spirits. Notably, leaves on their woody antlers sprout during springtime, grow dense during summer, change color in autumn, and fall off during winter.

The almost preternatural grace and beauty of this species belies the unusually loud and discordant noises it habitually makes. This has earned it the appellation of "The Trumpeting Lily" in popular culture. Brave individuals willing to invest in strong hearing protection are rewarded with a beautiful sight when they are able to catch a glimpse of this impressive specimen in the wild.
The Regal Ice Dragon prefers to hide in the ice caves of the northern lands. Being a solitary, peaceful dragon, the deeper, colder and more secluded the cave, the better.

Among good omens, few are considered more auspicious than the Affable Glowtail. Long ago, these cheery dragons were worshipped as spirits of fertility and new life. Today, they continue to be admired for their jovial demeanor and eagerness to bond with humans. *See Footnote.

Lady Pepper's Anthology of Dragons notes, "It was the teeth of a Machiavelli's Dragon that slayed the last descendant of Hans the Hunter and Hanna the Huntswoman. Although this species is one of the cleverest of dragons, it is doubtful that this particular prey required much of its mental acuity."

Amateur dracologists regularly mistake the call of this dragon for the more docile Tranquil Wyrm. This misapprehension rarely lasts terribly long; a key differentiator is that the call of the Colossus ends with an undulating fricative that is notably absent in that of the Tranquil Wyrm.
